neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert. Shows flat affect. MoCA 21/30: executive tasks severely impaired (trails 0/1, letter fluency — 5 F-words), memory (3/5 delayed recall), attention 5/6. He describes his bank termination as 'politics' and his prior neurologist's MCI diagnosis as 'overreaction.' Prominent anosognosia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal except: subtle reduced blink rate (possible PD feature). No supranuclear gaze palsy.
neurological_exam.motor: Mild right-sided rest tremor (4 Hz, PD-consistent). Mild cogwheel rigidity RIGHT wrist. Bradykinesia mild right. LEFT SIDE: minimal involvement — mild finger-tap slowing only. No alien hand phenomenon. Strength 5/5 bilaterally.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ symmetric. No Babinski. No Hoffman. Bilateral palmomental reflexes present.
neurological_exam.coordination: Mild right imprecision consistent with PD bradykinesia.
neurological_exam.gait: Right-sided Parkinsonian gait — reduced right arm swing, mild right-sided shuffle. LEFT arm swing preserved. Normal stride length. No festination.
neurological_exam.additional: His cognitive-behavioral syndrome has been attributed to Parkinson's disease dementia or PD-MCI by prior clinicians. He has a 4-year history of Parkinson's disease with mild, levodopa-responsive motor features. The behavioral syndrome — disinhibition, perseveration, and loss of social cognition — preceded or occurred at the same time as his PD diagnosis.

patient.chief_complaint: Cognitive and behavioral decline attributed to Parkinson's disease — 20 months progressive; behavioral features discordant with PDD pattern
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. N is a 52-year-old investment banker, terminated 20 months ago, who has been followed by a general neurologist for Parkinson's disease (diagnosed 4 years ago, mild right-sided onset). He was referred to the cognitive neurology clinic after his primary neurologist expressed concern that the cognitive and behavioral changes 'don't fit the expected pattern for PD-MCI.' He was initially diagnosed with PD-MCI by a prior neurologist 2 years ago and has been managed with carbidopa/levodopa with good motor response. His wife of 2 years — he married her during the period of behavioral changes — is the primary informant. She describes behaviors that preceded their marriage and were not apparent to her at the time: he made several large, impulsive financial decisions shortly before they met that his family has since described to her as completely uncharacteristic. He spent $180,000 on a collection of vintage motorcycles within 6 months, despite having no prior interest in motorcycles. He was terminated from his bank position for 'performance and conduct issues' — he had made unauthorized client fund transfers and made multiple sexually inappropriate comments to a junior colleague. He denied all of these events and filed an unsuccessful wrongful termination suit. He is now in a persistent legal battle over a disputed real estate transaction he initiated. At home, he has a highly rigid routine — he eats the same three items for breakfast in identical order each day and becomes enraged if the sequence is altered. He has stopped reading financial news, which was his lifelong obsession. He has no insight into any of these behaviors. Importantly, his motor PD symptoms have remained mild and respond well to levodopa. His father has Parkinson's disease and advanced cognitive impairment (in a memory care facility at age 82). His behavioral profile is notable for disinhibition, perseveration, loss of empathy, and impulsive financial decisions, occurring on a background of mild, levodopa-responsive Parkinson's disease.

findings.finding: Markedly impaired. Poor performance on set-shifting (Trail Making Test B), abstraction/similarities, and response inhibition; perseverative errors on Wisconsin-style sorting. Pattern consistent with dorsolateral and orbitofrontal dysfunction.
Reduced letter (phonemic) fluency out of proportion to category fluency — a frontal/executive signature rather than a semantic-store deficit.

Impaired emotion recognition (Ekman faces) and deficits on theory-of-mind / faux-pas tasks, with reduced affective empathy on the Interpersonal Reactivity Index — supports the bvFTD social-cognitive phenotype.
Relatively spared. Encoding and free recall reduced in a dysexecutive (retrieval) pattern, but recognition and cued recall are comparatively preserved.
Preserved. Copy of complex figure and clock contour intact; errors, when present, reflect poor planning rather than a perceptual or constructional deficit.
Fluent with intact single-word comprehension and confrontation naming largely preserved; no agrammatism or semantic loss — argues against a primary progressive aphasia variant.
Reduced insight (anosognosia), stimulus-bound responses, and reduced concern for test performance noted during the session.

Flat affect and prominent anosognosia. Bradyphrenia may contribute to processing speed, but executive and social-cognition impairment with loss of insight is disproportionate to the degree of slowing.

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not indicated in the standard FTD workup once a structural MRI and FDG-PET (or amyloid PET) have characterised the lobar pattern.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.

sequence_constraints.reason: Exclude structural cause of focal cognitive symptoms and screen for elevated ICP before lumbar puncture.

critical_actions: Recognise that PD-MCI does not fully explain the behavioural Rascovsky phenotype — bvFTD must be considered.
Pursue genetic testing — C9orf72/MAPT can cause FTD-parkinsonism overlap.
Optimise levodopa; avoid AChE inhibitors and minimise antipsychotics.
Apply Rascovsky 2011 bvFTD criteria explicitly (≥3 of 6 core features within 3 years) and document functional decline.
Assess and document decision-making, financial, and driving capacity given the high risk of impulsivity and impaired judgment in FTD.
Provide caregiver education, safety planning, and referral to FTD-focused support resources.
Offer genetic counselling and discuss cascade testing options if a pathogenic variant is identified or suspected.
contraindicated_actions: Do not start acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Do not start memantine: no evidence of benefit in bvFTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
key_reasoning_points: Overt parkinsonism with prior PD diagnosis justifies DaTscan in this case — it is NOT useless here, contrary to the general FTD rule.
Behavioural phenotype atypical for PDD; lobar imaging pattern supports FTD overlap.
C9orf72 expansion or MAPT mutation can produce FTD–parkinsonism.

red_herrings.data_point: Prior diagnosis of Parkinson's disease 4 years ago with motor response to levodopa
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors entire syndrome on PDD as explanation.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Concurrent PD does not explain the behavioural Rascovsky phenotype; FTD must be considered in parallel.

metadata.notes: Diagnostic puzzle bvFTD — C9orf72 with Parkinsonism, masquerading as PDD. Key teaching: DaTscan cannot distinguish PDD from FTD-Parkinsonism; FDG-PET posterior preservation rules out PDD; cholinesterase inhibitors contraindicated even in PD patient when FTD is primary diagnosis.
